set.stem: A 63-year-old man with COPD has progressive breathlessness, a raised JVP and pedal oedema. When clinically stable, his PaO2 on air is 7.1 kPa (53 mmHg) and his haematocrit is 0.49. Which therapy prolongs survival?
set.explanation: He has cor pulmonale (right heart failure from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) with a resting PaO2 below 7.3 kPa, so long-term oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours a day is indicated and is the only listed treatment that improves survival (MRC and NOTT trials); it also slows progression of pulmonary hypertension. Diuretics relieve oedema but do not change prognosis, ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers have no survival benefit in cor pulmonale, maintenance steroids cause harm and theophylline only modestly relieves symptoms. He must not smoke with oxygen in the home.

why: Stem lacked the resting PaO2 needed to justify LTOT; PaO2 7.1 kPa added and haematocrit given in SI form
Same idea and level as airway-0056 (older lifelong smoker with cough, sputum and breathlessness — diagnose COPD)

set.explanation: In every patient admitted with a COPD exacerbation, arterial blood gases should be measured (and the inspired oxygen noted) to detect hypercapnia and acidosis, guide controlled oxygen to a target SpO2 of 88–92% and decide whether NIV is needed; they are repeated 30–60 minutes after any change in oxygen. Spirometry, peak flow and full lung function tests are unreliable during an exacerbation and are done when stable, and CT is reserved for specific questions such as suspected pulmonary embolism or cancer.

set.stem: A 68-year-old woman with known COPD is admitted with increasing breathlessness, wheeze and sputum production. Her respiratory rate is 26/min and SpO2 is 84% on air; an arterial blood gas sample is being taken. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
set.explanation: She is hypoxaemic, so oxygen is the immediate priority, but in COPD it must be controlled: a 24% (or 28%) Venturi mask titrated to SpO2 88–92% (BTS), because high concentrations such as 60% worsen hypercapnia through loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q mismatch) and the Haldane effect. Oral steroids and antibiotics (for purulent sputum) follow promptly, and NIV is started only if the ABG shows persistent respiratory acidosis after optimal medical therapy.

why: Stem gave no saturation, so steroids or antibiotics were equally defensible; SpO2 84% on air added to make controlled oxygen the immediate step

set.stem: A child is admitted with a cough productive of thick, foul-smelling green sputum. His mother has noticed episodes of him coughing up blood. On examination he has marked finger clubbing and coarse crackles at both lung bases. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
set.explanation: Chronic purulent sputum, haemoptysis, bilateral coarse crackles and clubbing indicate bronchiectasis, and in a child the commonest cause in the UK is cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive CFTR mutations causing thick secretions and chronic infection). An inhaled foreign body causes localised, usually unilateral changes, and severe measles or whooping cough can cause post-infective bronchiectasis but are acute infections, not an explanation for this picture on their own. Confirm with a sweat chloride test and CFTR genotyping.

High-resolution CT is the diagnostic test for bronchiectasis: bronchi wider than the accompanying artery (signet ring sign), lack of tapering, visible airways within 1 cm of the pleura and bronchial wall thickening. The chest X-ray is often normal or non-specific. Sputum culture, sweat test (for cystic fibrosis), immunoglobulins, Aspergillus serology and bronchoscopy help to find the cause or organism but do not confirm the diagnosis.

A pulmonary exacerbation of cystic fibrosis should be treated promptly with antibiotics chosen from recent sputum cultures, usually a 14-day IV course of two anti-pseudomonal agents (e.g. ceftazidime plus tobramycin) for moderate or severe exacerbations, with intensified airway clearance physiotherapy. Mucolytics such as dornase alfa are maintenance treatments, corticosteroids are not routine (except in ABPA) and aminophylline has no role. CFTR modulators such as elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor reduce exacerbations long term.

set.stem: A teenager presents to the GP with symptoms suggestive of cystic fibrosis, and a sweat test is performed. Which result is diagnostic?
options: A chloride value of 60 mmol/L or above
set.explanation: Defective CFTR chloride channels prevent chloride reabsorption in the sweat duct, so sweat chloride is high. A sweat chloride of ≥60 mmol/L (confirmed on a second sample) with a compatible clinical picture or positive newborn screen is diagnostic; 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate and needs CFTR genotyping or further testing, and below 30 mmol/L makes CF unlikely. Sweat sodium is not used for diagnosis because it is less discriminating.

why: Source key (sweat sodium >60 mmol/L) is outdated; diagnosis is based on sweat chloride ≥60 mmol/L, so options updated to current cut-offs
Same idea and level as airway-0017 (current smoker with COPD — most important treatment is smoking cessation)
Same idea and level as airway-0081 (COPD breathless on SABA with no asthmatic features — add LABA+LAMA)

set.explanation: Purulent green sputum with wheeze, a modest CRP rise and no consolidation is an infective exacerbation of COPD, and Haemophilus influenzae is the commonest bacterial cause, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis; viruses such as rhinovirus trigger many exacerbations. The raised bicarbonate reflects renal compensation for chronic CO2 retention. Klebsiella and Staphylococcus aureus cause pneumonia rather than typical exacerbations. Suitable first-line oral antibiotics are amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin.

This is a non-infective exacerbation: breathlessness has increased, but the sputum is unchanged in volume and colour, there are no signs of pneumonia and he is not severely unwell. NICE NG115 recommends oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 5 days (GOLD 2025: 40 mg for 5 days) with more frequent short-acting bronchodilator, and antibiotics only when sputum becomes purulent or there is clinical evidence of pneumonia. Longer steroid courses add adverse effects without benefit, and furosemide is only for fluid overload.

In COPD with persistent breathlessness on a short-acting bronchodilator and no asthmatic or steroid-responsive features (no previous asthma diagnosis, raised blood eosinophils, substantial FEV1 variation or diurnal PEF variability), NICE NG115 and GOLD 2025 recommend a LABA+LAMA combination inhaler. An ICS-containing inhaler is added only when there are asthmatic features or exacerbations with blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL, because ICS increases pneumonia risk. LTOT is assessed only when resting SpO2 is ≤92% on air, and a single LABA is less effective than dual bronchodilation.

why: Parse fragment: first part of the stem of airway-0083 (question rejoined there)

set.stem: A 69-year-old man with COPD presents to the emergency department with breathlessness. Three days ago his GP started amoxicillin and prednisolone. In the department he has received back-to-back nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, inspired oxygen has been titrated to 28% to achieve SpO2 88–92%, and because of a poor response an aminophylline infusion has been started. Thirty minutes later, his ABG on 28% oxygen shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 7.6 kPa and PaO2 8.1 kPa. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
set.explanation: Respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >6.5 kPa) persisting despite optimal medical therapy is the indication for NIV (BTS/NICE), which reduces mortality and the need for intubation; a ceiling-of-treatment decision should be documented at the same time. His oxygenation is already on target, so reducing to 24% would risk hypoxaemia without treating ventilatory failure, and increasing to 35% would worsen hypercapnia. IV magnesium is for acute asthma, and IV hydrocortisone adds nothing to three days of oral prednisolone.

why: Stem rejoined from two parse fragments (airway-0082 and this item, missing PaO2 digit restored as 8.1 kPa); source key (reduce oxygen to 24%) is wrong because SpO2 is already 88–92% and persistent acidosis needs NIV

set.stem: A 75-year-old man with a body mass index of 31 kg/m2 has had worsening breathlessness and cough for about 1 week. He is normally short of breath and has had to give up walking to the shops, only 300 m away, and has a chronic cough that is worse in the morning. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day until this illness. ABG on air: pH 7.24, PaO2 6.2 kPa, PaCO2 9.8 kPa, HCO3− 33 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A long-term smoker with chronic morning cough and exertional breathlessness who deteriorates over a week has an exacerbation of COPD. The ABG shows acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure: severe hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with acidosis, and a raised bicarbonate that shows chronic CO2 retention with renal compensation. Obstructive sleep apnoea (or obesity hypoventilation) does not explain the chronic productive cough and acute deterioration, while acute asthma, pulmonary embolism and pulmonary oedema usually lower PaCO2 through hyperventilation. He needs controlled oxygen and early NIV.

set.stem: You review a 56-year-old man with COPD who is having an acute exacerbation. Which of the following features would suggest suitability for non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP?
set.explanation: NIV (BiPAP) is indicated for a COPD exacerbation with persistent respiratory acidosis from hypercapnia (pH <7.35, PaCO2 >6.5 kPa) despite optimal medical treatment, in a patient who is conscious and able to protect the airway. Confusion or a reduced conscious level, profound hypoxaemia, an undrained pneumothorax, vomiting, copious secretions and facial trauma are contraindications or signs that invasive ventilation is more appropriate. A pneumothorax must be drained before NIV.

why: Source key (confusion) is a contraindication to NIV; hypercapnia without profound hypoxia is the indication

set.stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD asks about home oxygen therapy. In which of the following settings have randomised controlled trials shown that long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) reduces mortality?
options: Cor pulmonale caused by chronic airflow obstruction
set.explanation: The MRC (1981) and NOTT (1980) trials showed that LTOT for at least 15 hours a day improves survival in hypoxaemic COPD, many of whose patients had cor pulmonale; the LOTT trial found no benefit in moderate desaturation. In cystic fibrosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and sarcoidosis oxygen may relieve breathlessness but has not been shown to prolong life, and asthma rarely causes chronic hypoxaemia. NICE criteria are a stable PaO2 <7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8.0 kPa with polycythaemia, peripheral oedema or pulmonary hypertension, in a non-smoker.

set.stem: A 66-year-old retired boilermaker attends the respiratory clinic. Spirometry shows post-salbutamol FEV1 1.81 L and FVC 2.7 L; transfer factor is 55% of predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 1.81/2.7 = 0.67, below 0.70, confirming persistent airflow obstruction, and the reduced transfer factor points to emphysema, so the diagnosis is COPD. Asbestos exposure in a boilermaker suggests pleural plaques or asbestosis, but plaques do not affect lung function significantly and asbestosis and other pulmonary fibrosis cause restriction with a normal or raised ratio. Asthma would be expected to show reversibility and preserved gas transfer, and pulmonary embolism does not cause obstruction.
